fact: In July 2025 Windsor's town manager told the Town Board the first plan was to convert two grass fields to artificial turf for a little over $2 million, and said Chimney Park already had one artificial turf field that staff was really happy with and that could host soccer and football as well as baseball.
quote: The initial plan would be for two grass fields to be converted to artificial turf, Hale said. … He put the cost for the turf for the two fields at “a little north of $2 million.” Chimney Park already has one artificial turf field “and staff is really happy with it,” Hale said. It can be used for soccer and football as well as baseball, he said.
source_label: BizWest, With loss of Future Legends, Windsor mulls millions for sports fields (July 27, 2025)
notes: bizwest.com returns 403 to automated fetches; the article text was read verbatim from the Wayback Machine capture of the same URL (web.archive.org/web/20251004035548/...). The two-field conversion that followed is windsor-co.chimney-park-turf-2026 (Windsor Project Connect, $2,240,000 budget, complete May 11, 2026).

fact: In July 2025 Windsor's deputy town manager described a lack of field space in Windsor and Northern Colorado, said the town had no town-owned or town-operated lighted fields, and said town athletics would not use the Future Legends complex because its playing conditions were unsafe and unplayable.
quote: “What we’re facing is a complex problem,” Windsor’s deputy town manager Eric Lucas said, “ a problem of lack of field space in Windsor and in Northern Colorado.” … But Windsor has no town-owned or -operated lighted fields. … “… We will not use Future Legends (for town-organized athletics) — not because we don’t have access, but because the playing conditions are unsafe and unplayable.”
source_label: BizWest, With loss of Future Legends, Windsor mulls millions for sports fields (July 27, 2025)
notes: Read verbatim from the Wayback Machine capture of 2025-10-04 (bizwest.com blocks automated fetches).

fact: Windsor developer Martin Lind argued in the same 2025 debate for plain grass fields first, saying there was no grass available and the town should build 20 or 30 acres of grass and let kids play.
quote: “There’s just no grass available. I’d like to see Windsor put some grass in for the kids,” Lind said. … “Instead, just build 20 or 30 acres of grass and let ’em go play. Then build it as it grows.”
source_label: BizWest, With loss of Future Legends, Windsor mulls millions for sports fields (July 27, 2025)
notes: Read verbatim from the Wayback Machine capture of 2025-10-04.

fact: In 2021 the City of Fort Collins' parks page said its turf fields are grass and the City has no artificial or synthetic fields, and it listed standing water, slippery or unsafe fields, turf tearing underfoot and drought-related conditions as reasons to cancel play.
quote: Some of the following are reasons to cancel: Standing Water on the Field(s) Fields are Slippery or Unsafe Turf Tears Underfoot Drought Related Conditions … 2021 Turf List (subject to change) *Turf Fields are grass; the City does not have any artificial/synthetic fields.
source_label: City of Fort Collins Parks, Park Rentals: Turf & Ballfield Reservations (Wayback Machine capture, Oct. 21, 2021)
notes: The live fcgov.com turf page now redirects to a general parks page on fortcollins.gov, which does not repeat the grass-only line; the same sentence was on the 2019 turfandballfieldinfo.php page. The 2025 Sports Field Policies PDF lists no synthetic field. Say 'in 2021' when citing, and re-check whether the City has added a synthetic field.

fact: Fort Collins' 2025 sports field rules schedule organized use from the third weekend in March through the first weekend in November and start games later in March, April, October and November to allow for frost.
quote: FIELD USE SEASON (MID-MARCH- First Sunday in NOVEMBER) Fields will not be scheduled and should not be used by organized groups prior to the third weekend in March and after the first weekend in November, unless otherwise approved, in writing, by the Director of Parks. … Later start times in the wing months allow for frost conditions and light to prepare the fields safely. … Game Start Time: 8:00am (wing months-Mar/Apr & Oct/Nov – 9:00am to allow for frost conditions)
source_label: City of Fort Collins Parks, 2025 Sports Field Policies & Procedures (Wayback Machine capture, Aug. 26, 2025)
notes: fcgov.com and fortcollins.gov return 403 to curl; the PDF was read from the Wayback capture. A 2026 edition was not found.

fact: Fort Collins' 2025 sports field rules tell teams to cancel for standing water, slippery or unsafe fields, or turf that tears underfoot or an infield that would rut, and allow each ballfield team one scheduled 1.5-hour practice a week against two for teams on grass turf fields.
quote: Examples of when fields should be cancelled: • Standing water on the field(s) • Fields are slippery or unsafe • Turf tears underfoot / use of infield would cause ruts … • Ballfield/diamond sports practices will be allowed ONE (1) scheduled practice per week/per team for 1.5 hours. • Turf sport practices will be allowed TWO (2) scheduled practices per week/per team for 1.5 hours.
source_label: City of Fort Collins Parks, 2025 Sports Field Policies & Procedures (Wayback Machine capture, Aug. 26, 2025)
notes: In the City's usage 'turf sports' means soccer-type sports on its grass fields, not synthetic turf.

fact: Fort Collins Utilities' 2020 Water Shortage Action Plan lets City parks and other owners of athletic fields on treated water get a permit to water up to 1.25 inches a week at Action Level I and 1.0 inch at Level II, to protect heavily used fields and keep them safe, and issues no such permits at Level III.
quote: This permit is to establish a custom watering schedule for City parks and areas owned by other entities that consist of playing and athletic fields that use treated water. … These areas are subject to less restriction in order to protect more actively used landscapes and maintain safety for those using the areas. … Action Level I: Average maximum of 1.25 inches or 0.78 gallons per square-foot per week. May water any day, as defined within a permit; no watering between the hours of 10 a.m. and 6 p.m. Action Level II: Average maximum of 1.0 inches or 0.47 gallons per square-foot per week. May water any day, as defined within a permit; no watering between the hours of 10 a.m. and 6 p.m. Action Level III: No permits will be issued.
source_label: Fort Collins Utilities, 2020 Water Shortage Action Plan (effective May 1, 2020), City and Community Active Areas Permit (Wayback Machine capture, Oct. 8, 2025)
notes: The Utilities water-shortage page (captured 2025-10-08) links this plan as current. The plan's Level II gallons figure (0.47) matches its Level II figure for inactive areas at 0.75 inch, so it looks like a typo; pages quote the inches only. In 2026 Fort Collins declared a voluntary Water Shortage Watch (fcu-water-shortage-watch-2026), not an Action Level.

fact: Fort Collins Utilities' 2020 Water Shortage Action Plan sets lawn watering at a target of 1 inch a week at Action Level I (a projected 1–15% shortage), 0.75 inch at Level II (16–25%) and zero at Level III (26–35%).
quote: Action Level … I - Low … II - Medium … III - High … % Projected Water Shortage … 1-15% … 16-25% … 26-35% … Lawn Watering … Target: 0.62 gallons/sq. ft. or 1" per week … Target: 0.47 gallons/sq. ft. or 0.75" per week … Requirement: 0 gallons/sq. ft. per week
source_label: Fort Collins Utilities, 2020 Water Shortage Action Plan (effective May 1, 2020), Action Summary Table (Wayback Machine capture, Oct. 8, 2025)
notes: Read from the table on p. 12 of the plan; the quote strings the table's cells together in column order. The Water Shortage Watch column also shows a 1-inch lawn target. Pairs with fc-wsap-athletic-fields (fields: 1.25 inches at Level I, 1.0 at Level II, no permits at Level III).

fact: Fort Collins' water shortage plan says most Poudre School District athletic fields are irrigated with treated water from Fort Collins Utilities.
quote: Most of PSD’s athletic fields are irrigated by treated water provided by Utilities.
source_label: Fort Collins Utilities, 2020 Water Shortage Action Plan (effective May 1, 2020), Communication Plan (Wayback Machine capture, Oct. 8, 2025)

fact: Western Resource Advocates' 2022 report cites a study finding a full-size natural grass sports field of 1.32 acres can use up to 1.5 million gallons of irrigation water a year depending on location, and the Synthetic Turf Council's estimate that a synthetic field the same size saves 500,000 to 1 million gallons a year.
quote: One study found that full-sized, 1.32 acre, natural grass sports fields can use up to 1.5 million gallons of water for irrigation per year depending on geographic location. The Synthetic Turf Council estimates that same-sized artificial turf athletic fields can save 500,000 to 1 million gallons of water per year (8.7 to 17.4 gallons/sq-ft)
source_label: Western Resource Advocates, Is Artificial Turf a Beneficial Water Conservation Tool in the West? (December 2022)
notes: WRA is a Colorado-based water policy nonprofit. The 1.5 million gallon figure is the study WRA cites, not a Northern Colorado measurement; the savings range is an industry (Synthetic Turf Council) estimate. Say both.

fact: Western Resource Advocates says schools often choose artificial turf because it allows continuous use while natural grass can need rest between activities, but that synthetic fields have needed heat-related closures, brushing and sanitizing, infill replacement and even irrigation for heat and playability.
quote: Regarding athletic fields specifically, many schools and universities choose to install artificial turf rather than natural grass fields because artificial turf is a durable play surface that allows for continuous use, while natural grass can require rest between athletic activities. Artificial turf can also save on maintenance costs associated with irrigation and mowing. However, artificial turf has been shown to require heat related closures, maintenance such as brushing and sanitization, regular replacement of infill material, and even irrigation to improve heat conditions and playability.
source_label: Western Resource Advocates, Is Artificial Turf a Beneficial Water Conservation Tool in the West? (December 2022)

fact: The U.S. Geological Survey defines an acre-foot as the water needed to cover an acre a foot deep, 325,851 gallons.
quote: acre-foot (acre-ft) --the volume of water required to cover 1 acre of land (43,560 square feet) to a depth of 1 foot. Equal to 325,851 gallons or 1,233 cubic meters.
source_label: U.S. Geological Survey Water Science School, Water Science Glossary

fact: At NOAA's Fort Collins station, March is the snowiest month of the year at 9.4 inches, April adds 6.2 inches of snow, and May is the wettest month at 2.72 inches of precipitation, with 5.8 days of a tenth of an inch or more (1991–2020 normals).
quote: USC00053005 FT COLLINS — MLY-SNOW-NORMAL 03 9.4 · 04 6.2 · 05 1.6 · MLY-PRCP-NORMAL 03 1.31 · 04 2.10 · 05 2.72 · MLY-PRCP-AVGNDS-GE010HI 05 5.8
source_label: NOAA NCEI U.S. Climate Normals 1991–2020, monthly, station FT COLLINS (USC00053005)
notes: Monthly snow normals for the other months: Jan 6.7, Feb 7.6, Nov 7.6, Dec 7.5, Oct 4.1, so March (9.4) is the peak; precipitation peaks in May (2.72). Station-to-town assignment by proximity, as in noaa-normals-fort-collins.

fact: At NOAA's Greeley UNC station, May is the wettest month at 2.65 inches of precipitation, with 5.6 days of a tenth of an inch or more, after 1.83 inches and 3.7 inches of snow in April (1991–2020 normals).
quote: USC00053553 GREELEY UNC — MLY-SNOW-NORMAL 03 5.1 · 04 3.7 · 05 0.5 · MLY-PRCP-NORMAL 03 0.91 · 04 1.83 · 05 2.65 · MLY-PRCP-AVGNDS-GE010HI 05 5.6
source_label: NOAA NCEI U.S. Climate Normals 1991–2020, monthly, station GREELEY UNC (USC00053553)
notes: Station-to-town assignment by proximity, as in noaa-normals-greeley-unc.

fact: The Sports Turf Managers Association says native-soil grass fields, the most common kind at schools and parks, usually drain more slowly than synthetic turf, and that every grass field needs mowing, watering, fertilizing and time off from play, with aerifying once or twice a year to ease compaction.
quote: The most commonly constructed fields for schools and recreational use are native soil fields. These fields usually drain more slowly than synthetic turf and sand-modified fields, and a 1.5% crown is suggested for most fields. … All natural turfgrass fields are living, breathing organisms that require mowing, watering, fertilizing, time off from play, and depending upon disease and pests, the application of plant protectants. To help ease compaction from heavy play, fields may be aerified once or twice a year.
source_label: Sports Turf Managers Association, A Guide to Synthetic and Natural Turfgrass for Sports Fields
notes: The guide is undated in its text and speaks of rubber-infill synthetic turf; it says it does not cover baseball or softball fields. The PDF prints 'fi' as a ligature; the quote spells it out.

fact: The Sports Turf Managers Association says synthetic fields need the manufacturer's grooming (sweeping, dragging and watering), may need infill added every year to restore resiliency, and need a manager who can handle seam repair and snow removal, lists a special rubber-blade snow plow among optional equipment, and measures a field's shock absorption in Gmax.
quote: All synthetic turf manufacturers have recommended grooming practices. Generally, these include sweeping, dragging, and watering for a clean, uniform appearance. Depending upon use and weather conditions, a sand-rubber mix may need to be added annually to help restore the field’s resiliency. The sports turf manager will also need special knowledge in troubleshooting and minor repairs, such as seam repair and snow removal. … Optional: … • Special rubber blade snow plow … field hardness – the ability of a surface to absorb energy. Shock absorbing properties are measured in Gmax.
source_label: Sports Turf Managers Association, A Guide to Synthetic and Natural Turfgrass for Sports Fields
notes: The PDF breaks 'sand-rubber' across a line ('sandrubber'); the quote restores the hyphen and spells out the 'fi' ligature.

fact: The Sports Turf Managers Association suggests an infrared thermometer to monitor a synthetic field's surface and delay activity above a set temperature, noting some have set it at 125 degrees, and says natural grass rarely rises above 85 degrees.
quote: In these situations, it is strongly suggested that you purchase an infrared thermometer so that the surface temperatures can be monitored continuously and activity delayed if the temperature rises above a set level. Some have set this temperature at 125 degrees. … The temperature of natural grass rarely rises above 85 degrees Fahrenheit, regardless of air temperature.
source_label: Sports Turf Managers Association, A Guide to Synthetic and Natural Turfgrass for Sports Fields
notes: The 85-degree grass figure is STMA citing a USGA study.

fact: The Sports Turf Managers Association's infield guide says the clay in a skinned baseball or softball infield turns slick when wet and often causes rainouts, and in hot, dry months cracks and hardens into a dangerous sliding surface with unsafe hops; it calls water the most critical element of field management, says a sandier mix (70 to 75% sand is common at the recreational level) is more forgiving in rain, and says a grade of about 0.5 to 1% usually moves water off an infield.
quote: Clay particles, however, will be slick, slimy, and slippery when wet – and are often the cause of rainouts. In contrast, during hot, dry summer months, clay will dry out, crack, and harden – causing a dangerous sliding surface and creating potentially unsafe ball hops. … A field that is high in sand content, for example, will be more forgiving in rain situations and can also withstand significantly more wear and tear if there is a limited maintenance staff managing multiple facilities at a complex. Often at the recreational level, the sand content on a field may be between 70 – 75% while the silt and clay would total 25 – 30% of the mix. … The single most critical element in field management is water. Too many fields lack access to water and in turn fail to manage moisture by adding water to the infield skin. … A grade of about 0.5-1% is usually sufficient to move water laterally off an infield surface
source_label: Sports Turf Managers Association, Management of Skinned Infields (Jeff Langner; reviewed by the 2015 STMA Information Outreach Committee)

fact: A 2023 systematic review of 53 studies from 1972 to 2020 found most studies of new-generation turf (13 of 18) reported similar overall injury rates to grass, the largest share reported more foot and ankle injuries on turf, soccer players had similar knee and hip rates while high-level football players had more knee injuries on turf, and the few studies finding more injuries on grass were all funded by the turf industry.
quote: A total of 53 articles published between 1972 and 2020 were identified for study inclusion. Most studies on new-generation turf (13/18 articles) found similar overall injury rates between playing surfaces. When individual anatomic injury locations were analyzed, the greatest proportion of articles reported a higher foot and ankle injury rate on artificial turf compared with natural grass, both with old-generation (3/4 articles) and new-generation (9/19 articles) turf. Similar knee and hip injury rates were reported between playing surfaces for soccer athletes on new-generation turf, but football players, particularly those at high levels of competition, were more likely to sustain a knee injury on artificial turf than on natural grass. … Only a few articles in the literature reported a higher overall injury rate on natural grass compared with artificial turf, and all of these studies received financial support from the artificial turf industry.
source_label: Gould, Lostetter, Samuelson and Guyton, Lower Extremity Injury Rates on Artificial Turf Versus Natural Grass Playing Surfaces: A Systematic Review (American Journal of Sports Medicine, 2023; 51(6):1615-1621), PubMed abstract
notes: Read from the PubMed abstract (efetch). Level of evidence 3; the authors did not pool risk ratios because the studies differ too much.

fact: A 2022 meta-analysis of 7 studies found no overall difference in ACL injury risk for soccer on artificial turf versus grass, but a higher risk for female players in games on turf, and no significant difference for male players.
quote: Pooled ACL injury IRRs demonstrated no significant differences in overall ACL injury risk when playing soccer on AT compared with NG (IRR = 0.57 [95% CI, 0.21-1.53]; P = .31). A significantly increased risk of ACL injury in games played on AT compared with NG was detected for female (IRR = 1.18 [95% CI, 1.05-1.31]; P = .004) but not for male players (IRR = 1.18 [95% CI, 0.97-1.42]; P = .09).
source_label: Xiao, Lemos, Hwang, Sherman, Safran and Abrams, Increased Risk of ACL Injury for Female but Not Male Soccer Players on Artificial Turf Versus Natural Grass (Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine, 2022), PubMed abstract
notes: 7 articles: 3 professional, 3 collegiate, 1 youth. AT = artificial turf, NG = natural grass.

fact: A 2020 meta-analysis of 12 studies found fewer concussions on artificial turf than on grass in contact sports, most marked in rugby and American football, and no association between turf and head injury or concussion in soccer.
quote: Initial screening generated 42 publications, with 12 meeting criteria for inclusion. … The rate ratio (RR) of head injury and concussion was less on artificial turf compared with natural grass (RR=0.89, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.04) as was the rate ratio of concussion only (RR=0.72, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.89). … This difference was most marked for sports such as rugby and American football. However, artificial turf has no association with the incidence of head injury or concussion while playing soccer.
source_label: O'Leary, Acampora, Hand and O'Donovan, Association of artificial turf and concussion in competitive contact sports: a systematic review and meta-analysis (BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine, 2020), PubMed abstract
notes: The head-injury-and-concussion rate ratio's interval crosses 1; the concussion-only ratio's does not. Authors declared no competing interests.
